# Reference Architecture {#sec-vol3-app-reference-architecture}

This appendix is a reference for assigning responsibilities across an agentic machine learning system. Its maps connect task requirements to state owners, interfaces, and evidence obligations, so a design review can identify missing ownership without prescribing a particular implementation stack. The chapters teach the mechanisms; this reference helps a reader locate their boundaries and check the assumptions connecting them.

## How to Use This Appendix {.unnumbered}

Consult the entry matching the design decision or missing record:

- When a responsibility has no clear owner, @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-mapping maps it to a logical component.
- When deciding which mechanisms a task requires, @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles links contract conditions to design obligations.
- When an operation crosses component boundaries, @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-turn traces the records needed at each handoff.
- When choosing an execution boundary, @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-actuation collects the compatibility and isolation questions.
- When deciding where information lives and who may change it, @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-memory distinguishes state ownership and reconstruction contracts.
- When placing components or investigating a deployment symptom, @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-blueprint identifies assumptions and measurements to check.

The maps describe logical responsibilities. One process may implement several rows; distributing a row across services does not remove its ownership requirement.

## The Component Map {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-mapping}

A design can contain a tool gateway yet leave retry ownership undefined. Naming a component therefore does not establish its contract. The responsibilities in @tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-matrix identify the records or decisions that need an owner when that function is present.

| Logical component      | Responsibility                                                      | Boundary to verify                                                            | Teaching location             |
|:-----------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|
| Model service          | Produce a response under a declared invocation configuration        | Response status and usage do not certify task acceptance                      | @sec-vol3-foundation-model    |
| Context assembler      | Select the inputs delivered to each call                            | Source, applicability, and trust survive selection and transformation         | @sec-vol3-context-engineering |
| Serving memory         | Manage derived attention state and optional prefix reuse            | Reuse requires compatible, available state and permitted sharing              | @sec-vol3-kv-cache            |
| Durable stores         | Retain sources, memory records, and retrieval indexes               | Derived records preserve their source bindings and validity policy            | @sec-vol3-long-term-memory    |
| Tool gateway           | Mediate dispatch and correlate returned evidence                    | Arguments, authority, preconditions, and repeat semantics are separate checks | @sec-vol3-tool-calling        |
| Isolation envelope     | Enforce the execution boundary                                      | Resource reach and lifetime match the declared threat model                   | @sec-vol3-sandboxes           |
| Harness                | Own control state, admission, and outstanding work                  | Stopping continuation does not settle existing effects or charges             | @sec-vol3-agent-harness       |
| Trajectory log         | Preserve recovery-required decisions and evidence                   | Acknowledgment satisfies the failure domain promised before dispatch          | @sec-vol3-durable-execution   |
| Recovery policy        | Select permitted responses to incomplete or failed work             | Unresolved operations and residual duties retain owners                       | @sec-vol3-failure-recovery    |
| Evaluation             | Assess declared criteria with scoped evidence                       | Checks cover stated properties rather than all possible outcomes              | @sec-vol3-evaluation          |
| Optional learning path | Admit records for a stated training use and assess changed behavior | Operational logs do not automatically qualify as training data                | @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation |
| Optional delegation    | Assign bounded work and reconcile child outcomes                    | Delegation preserves authority limits, accounting, and responsibility         | @sec-vol3-multi-agent         |

: **Responsibility Map**: Logical components, their owned decisions, and the boundaries to check when those functions belong in a design. Rows do not prescribe separate services. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-matrix tbl-colwidths="[17,27,36,20]"}

For each applicable row, record the actual owner, its inputs and outputs, and the assumptions under which its boundary holds. Information-flow policy also crosses the rows: a permitted read can still disclose sensitive data through a later output or tool call. @Sec-vol3-security-taint-tracking develops the provenance and permitted-flow checks needed at those handoffs. No single row establishes end-to-end correctness.

## Selecting Responsibilities from the Task Contract {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles}

A short task can issue an irreversible action, while a long task can remain disposable and read-only. Horizon alone cannot select durability or recovery mechanisms. H·S·A identifies exposures to examine; the adopted task contract determines permitted effects, failure tolerance, resource limits, and completion evidence (@sec-vol3-intro-hsa). @Tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles records conditional obligations rather than minimum stacks for exposure levels.

| Contract condition                              | Design obligation                                              | Evidence or assumption to record                                               |
|:------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Iteration consumes bounded resources            | Enforce admission and stopping conditions outside model output | Units, per-call limits, reserved liability, and finalization allowance         |
| Work must survive a stated failure              | Retain the record and artifacts needed to recover              | Failure domain, acknowledgment rule, retention, and ownership transfer         |
| Later decisions reuse observations              | Preserve source bindings and applicability conditions          | Source version or freshness policy; treatment of unavailable evidence          |
| The task executes generated code                | Choose and enforce an execution boundary                       | Reachable interfaces, credentials, isolation assumptions, and reset contract   |
| The task writes shared state                    | Check current authority and concurrency conditions             | Target identity, version precondition, and source-side conflict behavior       |
| A dispatched effect can outlive its caller      | Preserve operation identity and reconcile its outcome          | Endpoint repeat contract, settlement evidence, and owner of an unknown result  |
| An effect cannot be fully undone                | Bound admission and retain residual duties                     | Required approval, permitted partial outcomes, and escalation responsibility   |
| Success requires more than a plausible response | Protect and apply the acceptance criteria                      | Evidence coverage, uncertainty, and authority to adopt the verdict             |
| Work is delegated or used for training          | Add the corresponding supervision or data-admission contract   | Child authority and liabilities, or intended learning use and split boundaries |

: **Contract-Driven Design Obligations**: Conditions that make particular responsibilities necessary. Several conditions can apply to one operation; none uniquely determines a deployment topology. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles tbl-colwidths="[27,34,39]"}

Apply the rows to operations and retained records, not merely to a task's largest exposure label. A local patch needs a workspace boundary; publishing it adds source-side authorization and concurrency requirements. Publication does not imply that reversal is safe, available, or equivalent to undoing its consequences. If the task does not permit publication, withholding that capability removes the need to manage that particular effect without removing obligations for local execution and evidence.

## One Turn Through the Architecture {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-turn}

A tool-using turn in a crash-recoverable task provides a bounded interface check. Assume that the harness owns admission, the endpoint exposes an operation contract, and the runtime retains the inputs required for its promised recovery. The sequence below follows one admitted model call and one proposed external operation; answer-only turns, parallel calls, and approval waits take different paths.

1. **Admit the turn.** The harness considers a `READY` trajectory, checks current grants and control state, and reserves the proposed bounded liability against actual consumption and existing reservations while preserving finalization resources. Admitted work moves to `CALLING_MODEL` (@sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine).
2. **Assemble the context.** The assembler selects applicable source material and observations within the input budget. Record the delivered input or retained artifact references needed by the recovery contract; a hash identifies content but cannot reconstruct missing bytes.
3. **Call the model.** The model service receives the call with an output ceiling and a deadline, reuses the cached prefix where it can (@sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree), and returns a proposal with a stop reason and token usage (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract). The log records the reply.
4. **Validate and grant.** The tool gateway validates the proposal and applies runtime policy to the session, target, operation, and current preconditions. A discovered descriptor does not confer permission (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-mcp). Calls requiring approval go to the approval gate before dispatch (@sec-vol3-controlplane-hitl).
5. **Write intent, then dispatch.** The trajectory log makes the intent durable under the declared storage failure domain before dispatch (@sec-vol3-persistence-wal). Where the workflow supplies a compensating operation, its recovery plan is recorded as well (@sec-vol3-sagas-architecture). The gateway dispatches under the task's enforced grant and execution limits, preserving a logical operation identity where the endpoint supports that retry contract (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege, @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency).
6. **Wait without holding more than needed.** The harness moves the trajectory to `WAITING_TOOL`. The serving memory decides whether the trajectory's attention state stays resident, is evicted and recomputed, or is offloaded for the length of the wait (@sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping).
7. **Record the outcome and shape the observation.** The gateway correlates returning evidence with its call, preserving known results, partial effects, or unresolved status. Late outcomes can matter for reconciliation even when they should not resume the model. The log records this disposition and the bounded observation (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming).
8. **Check progress and continue.** Recovery compares task-scoped observations with recent history to assess possible nonprogress (@sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs). The harness applies its guarded continuation or finalization decision. Evaluation assesses acceptance under the declared criteria, including any required residual-duty evidence; its final verdict need not be available when finalization begins (@sec-vol3-evaluation-contract).

At each handoff, the receiving owner needs an identity, applicable version, and disposition, not merely a text description of the preceding step. Diagnostic spans can correlate observed calls and outcomes, but only the records and artifacts covered by the durability contract support promised recovery. A final acceptance decision can occur after this turn and can require evidence from outside its trace.

## The Model Service {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-processor}

An interrupted response needs a different disposition from a complete proposal. The invocation contract therefore identifies the model and call configuration, input format, output limit, status, and available usage evidence (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract). Deadlines and cancellation specify what the client can stop admitting or consuming and what termination the provider confirms. A local timeout does not prove that generation stopped or that its charge is settled. Token usage is one accounting input; task budgets can also constrain money, elapsed time, tool work, and other resources.

Prefix caching is an optional performance facility rather than a correctness requirement. If it is available, record compatibility, sharing, residency, and routing assumptions before relying on its savings. Session affinity can improve reuse but can also concentrate load; a changed prefix can reduce hits without changing the task's validity. @Sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree supplies the reuse conditions, while @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-kv-cache supplies the memory-sizing model. Behavioral suitability still requires task-level evaluation independently of this interface contract.

## Context and Memory {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-memory}

An agent's state lives in several places that differ in who may write them, how long they last, and what maintains their validity. The architecture needs an owner for each, and it must distinguish a derived copy from its source (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}). @Tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-memory maps these responsibilities to components. The persistent-record roles in @tbl-vol3-memory-tiers further distinguish the claims and evidence retained in durable stores.

| State class              | Level | Component that owns it      | Who may write                             | Validity and maintenance contract                                      |
|:-------------------------|:-----:|:----------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Working context**      | $S_1$ | Context assembler           | Runtime assembles; the model consumes it  | Selection and validity policy apply to each delivered call             |
| **Attention state**      | $S_1$ | Serving memory              | Serving engine, derived from model inputs | Reconstruction needs retained inputs and compatible configuration      |
| **Workspace artifacts**  | $S_2$ | Workspace owner             | Tools under granted execution authority   | Lifetime, reset, and any checkpoint binding are explicit               |
| **Source artifacts**     | $S_3$ | The owning system           | Owners and granted tool writes            | Authoritative; change only through explicit writes                     |
| **Trajectory log**       | $S_3$ | Runtime history owner       | Authorized runtime writers                | Authoritative history remains reconstructible for promised retention   |
| **Agent-written memory** | $S_3$ | Durable stores (write path) | The model proposes; the runtime admits    | Admission, correction, supersession, expiry, and deletion by policy    |
| **Retrieval indexes**    | $S_3$ | Durable stores (indexer)    | Authorized indexing path                  | Freshness is explicit; rebuilding needs retained sources and procedure |

: **State Classes by Owner**: Where each class of agent state lives in the reference architecture, who may write it, and what keeps it consistent with the world. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-memory tbl-colwidths="[18,7,20,25,30]"}

Three architectural rules follow from the table. First, a trajectory log records the events captured under its durability and retention contract; it does not establish every claim made in a logged response. Second, reconstruction requires retained inputs and a compatible reconstruction procedure. An index can be rebuilt from available sources, but a preference or observation cannot be recovered merely because an agent originally wrote it. Losing its only retained evidence can change later behavior. Third, the model proposes writes through mediated tools; workspace containment and memory admission enforce different boundaries on those operations. The context assembler selects from these records, and the retrieval contract (@sec-vol3-persistent-governance) governs how durable information re-enters a call, preserving its applicability, provenance, and retrieval limitations.

## Tools and Sandboxes {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-actuation}

The tool gateway mediates requests and returning evidence; the isolation envelope constrains execution reach. The gateway validates arguments, applies session policy and action-time checks, dispatches permitted calls, and returns bounded observations. Retry behavior depends on operation semantics and the endpoint's supported identity, effect, and result contract. A timeout may remain unresolved; a key alone does not make repetition safe (@sec-vol3-tool-calling). The envelope enforces the implementation's permitted resource access, credentials, workspace effects, network reach, and resource use (@sec-vol3-sandboxes). Neither a grant nor a descriptor enforces those limits merely by naming them.

Envelope choice depends on required interfaces, the threat model, and the configured enforcement boundary. @Tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-sandboxes summarizes the decision factors developed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-envelope-choice; it does not assign universal timings or rank isolation strength by product name.

| Envelope                | Shared or trusted components                                                | Compatibility and resource questions                                                        |
|:------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Shared-kernel container | Host kernel and configured isolation controls                               | Which host interfaces, identities, mounts, and devices remain reachable?                    |
| User-space kernel       | Interposed application-kernel implementation and its host interface         | Does the toolchain use supported interfaces, and what does its actual I/O cost?             |
| MicroVM                 | Guest kernel, VMM/hypervisor boundary, configured devices and host services | What initialization, guest residency, I/O, and reset costs does the deployment incur?       |
| Restricted bytecode     | Execution runtime and exposed host imports                                  | Can the workload target this format, and are memory, execution, and import effects bounded? |

: **Envelope decision factors**: Startup, steady execution, residency, and teardown must be measured for the workload and configuration. Shared baseline memory is an implementation-dependent optimization, not a universal property of an envelope type. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-sandboxes tbl-colwidths="[20,35,45]"}

Provisioning also depends on lifetime policy. A warm lease, a fresh restore, and a verified reset are different events. Pool capacity needs an explicit reserve, replenishment concurrency, admission policy, and memory ledger; average arrival rate alone does not establish that an environment is ready when needed (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling).

Supporting services enforce distinct boundaries. A credential broker withholds selected secrets from the guest and checks authorized use, while task data and returned observations may still be sensitive (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-credential-brokering). Egress controls constrain actual routes, destinations, and supported request semantics; permitted requests can still carry inappropriate disclosures (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-network). Security develops provenance and information-flow policy for those remaining cases (@sec-vol3-security-taint-tracking).

## The Harness {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-orchestration}

The harness record connects an admitted call to its trajectory identity, current version, grants, budgets, pending work, and retained artifacts (@sec-vol3-controlplane-acb). Check that every writer of this record passes through guarded transitions. A model-proposed plan update must not directly grant authority, release a reservation, or mark an unknown effect settled.

The control interface distinguishes holding new work from terminating existing work. Pause, cancellation, approval, and resume each need an explicit disposition for outstanding calls and liabilities. An authenticated late result may settle an effect without becoming eligible input to an obsolete continuation. @Sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine supplies the transition guards; the reference-design question is which owner applies them when control requests and results arrive concurrently.

## The Durable Log and the Trace {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-observability}

A surviving event record is useful only if the required history and referenced artifacts also survive. The recovery interface specifies the authoritative history, acknowledgment rule, compatible checkpoint boundary, retained bytes, and ownership-transfer mechanism. An incomplete replica cannot establish that an absent intent was never dispatched. @Sec-vol3-persistence-migration develops the validation and fencing needed before a new owner admits work.

Diagnostic traces have a different contract. Sampling or redaction can be acceptable for measurement while making a record insufficient for recovery. For each retained field, distinguish its recovery, replay, and diagnostic uses, with the completeness and lifetime promised for each (@sec-vol3-persistence-compaction). One storage service can support several uses, but its most permissive sampling policy must not silently determine all of them.

## Recovery {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-recovery}

An unknown tool outcome enters recovery as an unresolved operation, not as a failed call that can automatically be repeated. The recovery interface needs operation identity, available source evidence, permitted repeat behavior, and the owner of any remaining duty. Where compensation is supported, record its template and binding rule before forward dispatch; bind returned resource identities only from adequate evidence (@sec-vol3-sagas-architecture).

Recovery also consumes authority and resources. Its contract specifies which retries, revised proposals, cleanup, or escalation remain permitted after normal model-directed admission stops. Progress detectors and dependency breakers can limit further work without establishing the fate of prior effects. @Sec-vol3-sagas-containment supplies those containment boundaries.

## Evaluation {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-evaluation}

An acceptance result needs a binding to the task contract, candidate version, checks, and evidence scope. Record the evaluator's authority to publish that result and the uncertainty or residual duties it leaves. @Sec-vol3-evaluation-contract defines the distinction between local checks and task acceptance; a completed trace alone satisfies neither.

The evaluation boundary protects grading logic and authoritative results from the acting agent and from candidate code executed during grading. Read-only test storage does not prevent in-process interference. Shared isolation infrastructure is possible under explicit credentials, execution, and observation boundaries; the fixture description must still state which production behaviors it omits.

## The Learning Loop {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-learning}

Training is optional. When a system learns from its trajectories, the data interface must bind each admitted artifact to its source, transformations, intended use, and split policy (@sec-vol3-trajectory-curation). A recovery log, an accepted task, and a usable policy target are different objects; none automatically qualifies as another.

The return path identifies the changed model and the behavioral evidence supporting its release. A changed policy may alter trajectory length, state use, and requested effects without acquiring additional authority. The existing runtime bounds still apply, and the release decision needs renewed evaluation rather than an assumption that training improves every task.

## Deployment and the Fleet {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-blueprint}

A logical component map does not prescribe machine pools. A model service may be remote or local; a harness worker may retain live state while relying on durable records for recovery. Hardware virtualization is one possible isolation boundary, not a property of every sandbox. Placement should name the trusted components, reachable services, failure domains, and credentials rather than equating separate hosts or networks with adequate protection.

Resources held throughout a trajectory depend on its lifetime, not merely the duration of one model call. Under stable flow, Little's law relates mean live trajectories to admitted arrival rate and mean lifetime (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-capacity; @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-queueing). That product is not a hard admission limit or a guarantee against reserve exhaustion: bursts, variability, outstanding work, and reclamation require additional accounting. Across agents, typed task envelopes carry scoped authority and budgets (@sec-vol3-multiagent-contracts), reservations account for concurrent spending (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-governance), and cancellation requires supervision of the work and effects it reaches (@sec-vol3-multiagent-backpressure).

Use @tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-failures to form diagnostic hypotheses, not to assign causes from symptoms alone. The same observed delay or cost increase can originate in several components; measurement must distinguish them before an intervention is justified.

| Symptom                                              | Pool            | Candidate explanation                                                           | Evidence to compare                                                                     | Relevant responsibility                                                    |
|:-----------------------------------------------------|:----------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Calls queue while accelerators sit idle**          | Model service   | Residency pressure, admission policy, or input starvation                       | Resident state, runnable requests, queue reasons, and available service                 | Serving memory and admission (@sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping)                  |
| **Cost per turn rises without longer contexts**      | Model service   | Reduced prefix reuse, longer outputs, or a changed route or tariff              | Cached input share, output usage, model route, and applicable prices                    | Call accounting and context layout (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging) |
| **Trajectories busy but going nowhere**              | Harness         | Activity without established task progress                                      | Repeated actions and state as signals, not proof of nonprogress                         | Recovery: progress detection (@sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs)                   |
| **Sandbox leases time out under bursts**             | Sandbox hosts   | Ready reserve exhausted under the configured replenishment and admission policy | Standby empty; queued admissions and restores                                           | Isolation envelope: pool sizing (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling)              |
| **Duplicate external effects after a restart**       | Harness and log | Missing intent, unsafe retry, or ineffective endpoint deduplication             | Authoritative intent history, logical operation identities, and endpoint effect records | Intent ordering and settlement (@sec-vol3-persistence-wal)                 |
| **A failing dependency drains budgets**              | Tool gateway    | Repeated admissions from one or several retry owners                            | Dependency-scoped outcomes and attempts grouped by logical operation and owner          | Retry ownership and containment (@sec-vol3-sagas-containment)              |
| **Retrieved facts contradict the workspace**         | Durable stores  | Stale retrieval, a changed workspace, or incompatible claim scopes              | Source versions, applicability, retrieval time, and workspace changes                   | Record validity (@sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation)                        |
| **Spending exceeds limits across a delegation tree** | Fleet           | Missing reservations, underestimated liability, or unreconciled late charges    | Actual, reserved, and newly admitted liability under the same accounting boundary       | Spending governance (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-governance)                 |

: **Deployment Diagnostic Leads**: Candidate explanations and evidence to compare before attributing a symptom. The rows identify investigation boundaries, not unique causes or automatic remedies. {#tbl-vol3-app-ref-arch-failures tbl-colwidths="[18,11,23,22,26]"}

## Summary {#sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-summary}

The reference is complete for a particular design when each applicable obligation has an owner, an interface, and stated assumptions. Components can be combined, distributed, or omitted when the task does not require their function. The remaining review is about the boundaries between them: preserved identities and evidence, current authority, resource liability, and responsibility for unresolved work.
